# Model Details

## Overview

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Model name** | TechForum Tag Recommender |
| **Base model** | `microsoft/codebert-base` |
| **Architecture** | RoBERTa encoder + classification head |
| **Task** | Multi-label text classification |
| **Output labels** | 300 Stack Overflow tags |
| **Total parameters** | 124,876,332 (~125M) |
| **Max sequence length** | 512 tokens |
| **Model size (fp32)** | ~480 MB |
| **Model size (fp16)** | ~240 MB |

---

## Architecture

The model is built on `microsoft/codebert-base`, a RoBERTa-based transformer jointly pre-trained on natural language and source code. The original pooler head is replaced by a two-layer sequence classification head:

```
Input: [CLS] title + body [SEP] code snippets [SEP]
         ↓
   CodeBERT Encoder  (12 layers · 12 heads · hidden size 768)
         ↓
   [CLS] token representation  →  shape: (batch, 768)
         ↓
   Linear(768 → 768)  →  GELU  →  Dropout(0.1)
         ↓
   Linear(768 → 300)
         ↓
   Sigmoid  →  per-label probabilities  →  shape: (batch, 300)
```

### Why CodeBERT?

CodeBERT was pre-trained on both GitHub source code and natural language documentation, making it uniquely suited for Stack Overflow questions that mix technical prose with code snippets. Compared to plain BERT or RoBERTa, CodeBERT produces richer representations of code-heavy inputs, which is critical for distinguishing tags like `python` vs `django` vs `flask` from the same question.

### Why Sentence-Pair Format?

The tokenizer encodes the question text and code as two separate sequences:

```
[CLS] title body [SEP] code [SEP]
 ↑                             ↑
Sequence A              Sequence B
```

This lets the encoder apply different segment embeddings to prose vs. code, preserving the semantic boundary between them rather than treating the whole input as a flat string.

---

## Training

### Loss Function — Asymmetric Loss (ASL)

Standard Binary Cross-Entropy treats all labels equally. In a 300-label multi-label problem, each question has on average only 2–3 positive labels, meaning ~297 labels are negative for every sample. This massive imbalance causes the model to be overwhelmed by easy negative examples and learn to predict nothing.

**Asymmetric Loss** solves this by applying different focusing exponents to positives and negatives:

$$\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{c}\left[ y_c \log(p_c)(1-p_c)^{\gamma_+} + (1-y_c)\log(1-\tilde{p}_c)\tilde{p}_c^{\gamma_-} \right]$$

Where $\tilde{p}_c = \min(p_c + m, 1)$ clips low-probability negatives by margin $m$.

| Parameter | Value | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `gamma_neg` | 4 | Strongly down-weights easy negatives |
| `gamma_pos` | 1 | Slight focus on hard positives |
| `clip` | 0.10 | Ignores very low-probability negatives |

### Training Configuration

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Optimizer** | AdamW |
| **Learning rate** | 2e-5 |
| **Weight decay** | 0.01 |
| **Warmup ratio** | 5% of total steps |
| **Epochs** | 2–5 (early stopping, patience=4) |
| **Per-device batch size** | 8 |
| **Gradient accumulation** | 8 steps |
| **Effective batch size** | 64 |
| **Precision** | FP16 mixed precision |
| **Gradient checkpointing** | Enabled |
| **Early stopping metric** | F1 Micro |
| **Eval / save frequency** | Every 1,000 steps |

### Per-Label Threshold Tuning

After training, each of the 300 labels receives its own optimal classification threshold via grid search on the evaluation set:

```
For each label c:
    τ*_c = argmax over τ ∈ [0.05, 0.95] of F1(y_c, ŷ_c(τ))
    (200 threshold candidates per label)
```

This consistently yields +1–3% micro-F1 over a single global threshold and allows the model to be more aggressive (lower threshold) on rare tags and more conservative on common ones.

---

## Model Files

| File | Description |
|---|---|
| `config.json` | Model architecture configuration |
| `pytorch_model.bin` | Model weights (fp32) |
| `tokenizer_config.json` | Tokenizer settings |
| `vocab.json` + `merges.txt` | BPE vocabulary (from CodeBERT) |
| `mlb.pkl` | MultiLabelBinarizer — maps predictions to tag strings |
| `tag_vocab.txt` | Plain-text list of all 300 tags (one per line) |
| `best_thresholds.npy` | Per-label classification thresholds — shape `(300,)` |
| `training_config.json` | Training metadata (samples, max_length, etc.) |

---

## Performance

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| **F1 Micro (per-label thresholds)** | ~0.75 |
| **Precision Micro** | ~0.74 |
| **Recall Micro** | ~0.76 |
| **F1 Head labels** (≥1000 train examples) | ~0.80+ |
| **F1 Tail labels** (<100 train examples) | ~0.45–0.60 |

Evaluated on 80,000 held-out Stack Overflow questions.

---

## Limitations

- Predicts only from a fixed vocabulary of **300 tags** — niche or new technologies are not covered
- Trained exclusively on **English** Stack Overflow questions
- Performance is lower on **rare tags** with few training examples
- Not suitable for non-software-development content
- Model knowledge is limited to the Stack Overflow Stack Sample dataset collection period

instances.overview: # Documentation ## What This Model Does **TechForum Tag Recommender** automatically suggests relevant tags for technical questions on developer forums. You give it a question title, body, and optional code — it returns a ranked list of tags from a 300-label vocabulary covering the most common Stack Overflow topics. **Example:** > *"React useState not triggering re-render when updating object"* > → `['reactjs', 'react-hooks', 'javascript']` The model is designed to assist users in tagging their posts correctly, improving discoverability and helping experts find questions relevant to their skills. --- ## Instance Overview A single inference instance consists of: | Component | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | `title` | `str` | ✅ Yes | The question title in plain text | | `body` | `str` | ✅ Yes | The question body in plain text (strip HTML) | | `code` | `str` | ❌ No | Extracted code snippets in plain text | The model returns a `list[str]` of predicted tags, sorted from highest to lowest confidence. Typical output length is 1–4 tags per question. **Tokenization format (internal):** ``` [CLS] title body [SEP] code snippets [SEP] ←— Sequence A ——→ ←— Sequence B ——→ (max 256 tokens total) ``` --- ## Quick Start ### 1. Install dependencies ```bash pip install transformers torch joblib numpy ``` ### 2. Download model files Download the full model folder from this page. It contains: - Model weights + tokenizer - `mlb.pkl` — label encoder - `best_thresholds.npy` — per-label decision thresholds ### 3. Run inference ```python import torch, joblib, numpy as np from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification model_dir = "techforum-tagger-final" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_dir) model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_dir) mlb = joblib.load(f"{model_dir}/mlb.pkl") thresholds = np.load(f"{model_dir}/best_thresholds.npy") device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu") model.to(device).eval() def predict_tags(title: str, body: str, code: str = "") -> list[str]: text = f"{title.strip()} {body.strip()}" inputs = tokenizer(text, code, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=256).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): probs = torch.sigmoid(model(**inputs).logits.squeeze()).cpu().numpy() preds = (probs >= thresholds).astype(int) tags = list(mlb.inverse_transform(preds.reshape(1, -1))[0]) if not tags: tags = [mlb.classes_[i] for i in np.argsort(probs)[::-1][:3]] return sorted(tags, key=lambda t: -probs[mlb.classes_.tolist().index(t)]) # Run it print(predict_tags( title="Docker container exits immediately after running", body="My Dockerfile builds fine but the container exits with code 0 right away.", code='FROM ubuntu:latest\nCMD ["echo", "Hello"]' )) # → ['docker', 'dockerfile', 'container'] ``` --- ## How It Works ### Step 1 — Text Preprocessing Before tokenization, the raw question body (HTML from Stack Overflow) is split into plain text and code snippets: ```python import re def extract_and_clean(html_body: str): code = " ".join(re.findall(r'(.*?)', html_body, re.DOTALL)) text = re.sub(r'.*?', '', html_body, flags=re.DOTALL) text = re.sub(r'<[^<]+?>', '', text).strip() return text, code ``` ### Step 2 — Tokenization Title + body are combined and encoded as sequence A. Code snippets are encoded as sequence B. CodeBERT's tokenizer handles the `[CLS]`, `[SEP]`, and segment embeddings automatically. ### Step 3 — Inference The encoder produces a `[CLS]` representation that the classification head maps to 300 logits. Sigmoid converts logits to independent probabilities per label. ### Step 4 — Threshold Decision Each label has its own threshold (tuned on the validation set) ranging from 0.05 to 0.95. A label is predicted positive if its probability exceeds its threshold. If no label passes its threshold, the top-3 labels by probability are returned as a fallback. --- ## Supported Tags The model covers the **300 most frequent Stack Overflow tags**. A few examples by category: | Category | Tags | |---|---| | Languages | `python`, `javascript`, `java`, `c#`, `c++`, `php`, `r`, `swift`, `kotlin`, `go` | | Web frontend | `html`, `css`, `reactjs`, `angular`, `vue.js`, `typescript`, `jquery` | | Web backend | `node.js`, `django`, `flask`, `spring-boot`, `asp.net`, `express` | | Data & ML | `pandas`, `numpy`, `tensorflow`, `pytorch`, `scikit-learn`, `matplotlib` | | Databases | `sql`, `mysql`, `postgresql`, `mongodb`, `sqlite`, `sql-server` | | DevOps | `docker`, `git`, `linux`, `bash`, `kubernetes`, `aws` | | Mobile | `android`, `ios`, `react-native`, `flutter` | Full tag list available in `tag_vocab.txt` inside the model folder. --- ## Inference Hardware Requirements | Setting | Requirement | Latency | |---|---|---| | **CPU** | 4 GiB RAM | ~300ms / question | | **GPU** | 4 GiB VRAM | ~12ms / question | | **Recommended (production)** | GPU with ≥ 4 GiB VRAM | ~12ms / question | FP16 inference can be enabled for ~2× memory reduction: ```python model.half() # convert to fp16 before inference ``` --- ## Training Data Trained on **800,000 Stack Overflow questions** from the [Stack Overflow Stack Sample](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/stackoverflow/stacksample) dataset (CC BY-SA 4.0), covering questions from Stack Overflow's public archive. Only questions containing at least one of the top-300 tags were included. | Split | Samples | |---|---| | Train | 720,000 | | Validation / Test | 80,000 | --- ## Evaluation Evaluated on the 80,000-sample held-out test set: | Threshold Strategy | F1 Micro | Precision | Recall | |---|---|---|---| | Fixed @ 0.40 | ~0.73 | ~0.71 | ~0.75 | | Fixed @ 0.50 | ~0.72 | ~0.75 | ~0.70 | | **Per-label tuned** | **~0.75** | **~0.74** | **~0.76** | --- ## Known Limitations | Limitation | Detail | |---|---| | Fixed vocabulary | Only 300 tags — new or niche technologies not covered | | English only | Trained on English Stack Overflow content | | Tail label gap | Rare tags (< 100 training examples) have significantly lower F1 | | Short questions | Very brief posts (< 10 words) produce less reliable predictions | | Dataset cutoff | Technologies popularized after the dataset collection date are underrepresented |
instances.usage:
# Example Use ## Installation ```bash pip install transformers torch joblib numpy ``` ## Load Model & Artifacts ```python import torch import joblib import numpy as np from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification model_dir = "techforum-tagger-final" # path to downloaded model folder tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_dir) model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_dir) mlb = joblib.load(f"{model_dir}/mlb.pkl") thresholds = np.load(f"{model_dir}/best_thresholds.npy") device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu") model.to(device).eval() ``` ## Predict Tags ```python def predict_tags(title: str, body: str, code: str = "") -> list[str]: """ Args: title : Question title (plain text) body : Question body (plain text, HTML already stripped) code : Code snippets (optional, plain text) Returns: List of predicted tag strings sorted by confidence (highest first) e.g. ['python', 'pandas', 'dataframe'] """ text = f"{title.strip()} {body.strip()}" inputs = tokenizer( text, code, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=256, ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): probs = torch.sigmoid(model(**inputs).logits.squeeze()).cpu().numpy() preds = (probs >= thresholds).astype(int) tags = list(mlb.inverse_transform(preds.reshape(1, -1))[0]) # Fallback: return top-3 if no tag exceeds its threshold if not tags: tags = [mlb.classes_[i] for i in np.argsort(probs)[::-1][:3]] return sorted(tags, key=lambda t: -probs[mlb.classes_.tolist().index(t)]) ``` ## Examples ### Python / Data Science ```python tags = predict_tags( title="Pandas SettingWithCopyWarning when updating a filtered DataFrame", body="I filter a DataFrame and update a column in the result, but Pandas " "raises SettingWithCopyWarning. I am unsure if my data is actually " "being modified or if I am working on a temporary copy.", code="df_filtered = df[df['age'] > 20]\ndf_filtered['status'] = 'adult'" ) print(tags) # → ['python', 'pandas', 'dataframe'] ``` ### JavaScript / React ```python tags = predict_tags( title="React useState not triggering re-render when updating object", body="My component does not re-render when I update a property inside " "a state object. I think it is related to how React checks for changes.", code="const [user, setUser] = useState({ name: 'John', age: 25 });\n" "const updateAge = () => { user.age = 26; setUser(user); };" ) print(tags) # → ['reactjs', 'react-hooks', 'javascript'] ``` ### Java ```python tags = predict_tags( title="String comparison using == returns false unexpectedly in Java", body="I am comparing two Java strings that have the exact same text, " "but == returns false. I am confused about how to properly check " "if their contents are identical.", code='String a = new String("test");\nString b = new String("test");\n' 'if (a == b) { System.out.println("Match!"); }' ) print(tags) # → ['java', 'string', 'equals'] ``` ### SQL ```python tags = predict_tags( title="SQL LEFT JOIN returning duplicate rows", body="I want one row per customer with their most recent order " "but I get duplicates. DISTINCT does not help.", code="SELECT c.name, o.order_date\n" "FROM customers c\n" "LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;" ) print(tags) # → ['sql', 'join', 'duplicates'] ``` ### No Code (text-only question) ```python tags = predict_tags( title="How to undo the last local commit in Git?", body="I accidentally committed changes to my local branch. " "I have not pushed to remote yet. How can I undo the commit " "but keep the file changes in my working directory?", ) print(tags) # → ['git', 'git-commit', 'undo'] ``` ## Input / Output Reference | | Type | Shape | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | `title` | `str` | — | Plain text, required | | `body` | `str` | — | Plain text (strip HTML first), required | | `code` | `str` | — | Plain text code snippets, optional | | Tokenized input | `torch.Tensor` | `(1, ≤256)` | Sentence-pair format | | Raw logits | `torch.Tensor` | `(1, 300)` | One per tag label | | Probabilities | `np.ndarray` | `(300,)` | After sigmoid | | **Output** | `list[str]` | `1–5 tags` | Sorted by confidence | ## Stripping HTML (if your input is raw Stack Overflow HTML) ```python import re def extract_and_clean(html_body: str): """Extract plain text and code snippets from a raw HTML body.""" code = " ".join(re.findall(r'(.*?)', html_body, re.DOTALL)) text = re.sub(r'.*?', '', html_body, flags=re.DOTALL) text = re.sub(r'<[^<]+?>', '', text).strip() return text, code body_html = "

I filter a DataFrame and get a warning.

df[df['a']>1]['b']=2" clean_text, code_snippets = extract_and_clean(body_html) tags = predict_tags( title="Your question title", body=clean_text, code=code_snippets, ) ```

## Heart Disease Prediction — Naive Bayes from Scratch

### Overview
A Naive Bayes classifier built entirely from scratch in pure Python
(no ML libraries). It predicts whether a patient has heart disease
based on 4 features: Age, Blood Pressure, Cholesterol, and Max Heart Rate.

### How It Works
- Continuous values are binned into categories (e.g. age → young/middle/old)
- Dataset is split: 70% training, 30% testing
- Uses Laplace smoothing to avoid zero probabilities
- Predicts the class with the highest posterior probability

### How to Use
dataset = load_data('heart_disease.csv')
train, test = split_dataset(dataset)
separated = separate_by_class(train)
predictions = get_predictions(separated, test)

### Language
Pure Python — no external ML libraries

# Model Summary

The **YOLO26n-pose** is a state-of-the-art, nano-scale real-time object detection and human pose estimation model. Built upon the Ultralytics YOLO architecture and exported to PyTorch (`.pt`), this model is specifically optimized for high-speed inference on edge devices and standard hardware without sacrificing keypoint accuracy. It detects human bounding boxes and skeletal keypoints simultaneously.

## Usage

This model is intended for developers and researchers building applications that require real-time human tracking, such as sports analytics, physical therapy monitoring, or interactive gaming.

**Code Snippet:**

```python
!pip install ultralytics > /dev/null 2>&1
import cv2
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from ultralytics import YOLO

# Load the model
model = YOLO('/kaggle/input/models/assemelqirsh/yolo26n-pose/pytorch/default/1/yolo26n-pose.pt')

# Run inference
results = model('https://ultralytics.com/images/bus.jpg')

# Display results
annotated_image = cv2.cvtColor(results[0].plot(), cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
plt.imshow(annotated_image)
plt.axis('off')
plt.show()

```

* **Inputs:** RGB Images or Video frames (standard shape: `[1, 3, 640, 640]`).
* **Outputs:** Bounding box coordinates `[x, y, w, h]`, confidence scores, and 17 human keypoints `[x, y, visibility]` per detected person.
* **Known Failures:** The model may struggle with heavy occlusions (e.g., people standing behind objects), highly unusual body contortions, or extremely crowded scenes where skeletons overlap.

## System

This is a standalone inference model. It can be easily integrated into broader downstream computer vision pipelines (like DeepSORT or ByteTrack for multi-target tracking over time) or action-recognition systems.

## Implementation requirements

* **Training Hardware:** Trained by Ultralytics utilizing multi-GPU cloud environments (specifically Amazon EC2 P4d instances equipped with NVIDIA A100 GPUs).
* **Software:** Python, PyTorch, and the Ultralytics library.
* **Inference Compute:** Highly efficient. Benchmarks show it achieves approximately 40.3 ms latency on standard CPUs (ONNX) and a lightning-fast 1.8 ms latency on a T4 GPU (TensorRT10).

# Model Characteristics

## Model initialization

The model was fine-tuned from pre-trained YOLO nano pose weights to accelerate convergence and improve generalized human detection before training on the target dataset.

## Model stats

* **Size:** Nano architecture (2.9 million parameters, 7.5 Billion FLOPs).
* **File Size:** ~8 MB.
* **Latency:** Highly optimized for edge deployment; exact latency depends on the deployment hardware but is designed for >30 FPS on standard GPUs.

## Other details

The model weights are provided in standard FP32/FP16 PyTorch format. It is not aggressively pruned or heavily quantized by default, though users can export it to OpenVINO, TensorRT, or TFLite (INT8) for further optimization using the Ultralytics export tools.

# Data Overview

## Training data

The model was pre-trained on the official COCO-Pose (COCO Keypoints val2017) dataset. This dataset features 17 specifically defined human body keypoints. Images were pre-processed using standard YOLO augmentations including mosaic, mixup, random scaling, and color-space adjustments to improve robustness.

## Demographic groups

The training data features a wide variety of human subjects as represented in the standard, crowd-sourced COCO dataset, capturing diverse individuals in everyday, real-world scenes.

## Evaluation data

Data was split using the standard COCO 2017 configuration (approximately 118,000 training images and 5,000 validation images).

# Evaluation Results

## Summary

The model was evaluated using standard Object Detection and Pose Estimation metrics.

* **Pose mAP50-95:** **57.2**
* **Pose mAP50:** **83.3**

## Subgroup evaluation results

No formal subgroup disaggregation analysis was performed. Users should be aware that pose estimation accuracy generally degrades for subjects further away from the camera or under poor lighting conditions.

## Fairness

Standard practices were observed to ensure a diverse representation of human subjects in the baseline data, but specific quantitative fairness metrics regarding skin tone or body type disparities were not formally baselined for this specific iteration.

## Usage limitations

* **Environmental:** Performance may drop in extreme low-light or severe weather (heavy rain/snow) if not represented in the training data.
* **Hardware:** While lightweight, achieving true real-time video processing requires hardware acceleration (GPU/NPU).

## Ethics

This model is designed for tracking human form and movement. Developers utilizing this model should ensure they comply with local privacy laws and regulations regarding surveillance and biometric tracking. It should not be used in systems designed to infer sensitive demographic traits, emotional states, or to facilitate unconsented surveillance.

## Disclaimer & Acknowledgments

**Note:** I am not the original creator or owner of this model. All underlying architecture, pre-trained weights, and intellectual property belong exclusively to **Ultralytics**. This model is uploaded here solely for community accessibility and ease of use within Kaggle notebooks.

For the official source code, comprehensive documentation, and commercial licensing inquiries, please visit the official Ultralytics pages:
* **Official Website:** [https://ultralytics.com](https://ultralytics.com)
* **GitHub Repository:** [https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics](https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics)

# MNIST CNN Classifier

This model is a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) built using TensorFlow and Keras for handwritten digit recognition on the MNIST dataset.

The model classifies grayscale images of handwritten digits (0–9) with high accuracy and demonstrates the effectiveness of deep learning for image classification tasks.

## Features

* TensorFlow/Keras implementation
* CNN architecture with multiple convolutional layers
* Batch Normalization and Dropout for improved generalization
* Trained on the MNIST dataset
* Achieves over 99% test accuracy
* Ready for inference and deployment

## Dataset

The model was trained on the MNIST handwritten digit dataset containing 70,000 grayscale images of size 28×28 pixels.

* Training Images: 60,000
* Test Images: 10,000
* Classes: 10 (Digits 0–9)

## Use Cases

* Handwritten digit recognition
* OCR learning projects
* Deep learning education
* Computer vision demonstrations
* CNN architecture studies

## Framework

TensorFlow / Keras

## License

Apache 2.0

instances.overview: This model accepts a grayscale image of shape (28, 28, 1) and predicts the probability distribution across ten digit classes (0–9). The digit with the highest probability is selected as the final prediction.
instances.usage:
from tensorflow.keras.models import load_model
import numpy as np

# Load model
model = load_model("mnist_cnn_model.keras")

# Preprocess image
image = image.reshape(1, 28, 28, 1)
image = image.astype("float32") / 255.0

# Predict
prediction = model.predict(image)
digit = np.argmax(prediction)

print("Predicted Digit:", digit)
